newsitem.title: UK: Rise in UK CJD cases may reflect better diagnosis.
newsitem.headline: Rise in UK CJD cases may reflect better diagnosis.

text.p: Cases of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) in England and Wales have increased since the early 1980s and the rise has been particularly pronounced in people over 70, according to an article in the British Medical Journal on Friday.
However, the increase appears to reflect better methods of monitoring the disease rather than any real change in incidence, the authors said.

Dr Bob Will of the CJD surveillance unit in Edinburgh and colleagues from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine reported that the yearly number of deaths from CJD rose to an average of 33.6 in the period from 1990 to 1996 from an average of 24.8 in the period 1980 to 1984.

Beef exports from Britain were banned by the European Union last year after the British government said there was a possibility that eating beef contaminated with brain-wasting "mad cow" disease might trigger a related disease, Creutzfeldt-Jakob, in humans.

Fears of mad cow disease have also risen sharply as fresh cases come to light, politicians face repeated questioning about the safety of British meat and scientists uncover more facts about the deadly disease.
The scientists said the old appeared most at risk.
"In the United Kingdom the greatest increase in incidence has been in people aged over 70," they wrote.
But they added that "age-specific time trends suggest that improved ascertainment may explain much or all of the apparent rise in the incidence of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease since 1970".
Unexplained, they say, is the existence of a group of comparatively young patients with CJD who have exhibited unusual neuropathological features.

"Were these cases really 'new' or had similar cases occurred previously without being identified? If these cases were new, why did they occur in the United Kingdom in the mid-1990s?" the authors asked.

Experiments with mice as well as fresh statistics on the incidence of CJD among humans should bring the medical community closer to determining definitively whether there is a link between CJD and bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), or 'mad cow' disease, they wrote.
